Add a `pattern="[0-9a-fA-F-]{10,11}"` (or normalize on submit) and ensure the registered value is normalized (dashes stripped) before submission.

findings.title: formatBackupCode is used before its declaration (temporal dead zone risk) and defined inside component body
findings.body: `formatBackupCode` is referenced at line 95 inside `handleSetup` (`body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)`) but is declared with `const` at line 163, AFTER the `handleSetup` function definition. Because `handleSetup` is only invoked at runtime (after the component has fully rendered and `formatBackupCode` is initialized), this works due to closure semantics — but it is fragile and confusing. If `handleSetup` were ever called during render or if the declaration order changed, it would throw a ReferenceError. Move `formatBackupCode` above `handleSetup` (or to module scope) for clarity and safety.

findings.title: backupCodes state is untyped (never[]) causing implicit any in map
findings.body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([])` infers type `never[]`. When `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` is called with `any` (from `response.json()`), TypeScript does not error because `any` is assignable, but `backupCodes.map((code) => ...)` at line 203 has `code` implicitly typed. This loses type safety — if the API shape changes, no compile error will catch it. Type the state as `useState<string[]>([])`.

findings.title: Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on unmount
findings.body: `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` creates `backupCodesUrl`, and it is revoked only when a NEW setup creates another URL (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). If the user closes the modal without re-running setup, or the component unmounts, the object URL is never revoked, leaking memory. Add a `useEffect` cleanup that revokes `backupCodesUrl` on unmount.

findings.title: Backup code and TOTP code are both registered in the same form and both submitted, allowing ambiguous server-side branch selection
findings.body: The login form registers both `totpCode` (via TwoFactor's hidden input) and `backupCode` (via BackupCode's TextField) in the same react-hook-form. When the user switches between TOTP and backup-code modes (via the 'Lost access' / 'Go back' buttons), the code clears the other field with `methods.setValue("totpCode", "")` or `methods.setValue("backupCode", "")`, but `setValue` does not trigger re-validation or necessarily clear the DOM input value for uncontrolled inputs. On submit, `signIn` sends ALL form values including `email`, `password`, `totpCode`, `backupCode`, and `csrfToken`. The server-side logic in `next-auth-options.ts` checks `credentials.backupCode` FIRST — so if a stale `totpCode` value remains in the form state (e.g. user typed a TOTP, switched to backup code, the setValue didn't clear the hidden input's value), the server may receive both and take the backup-code path even though the user intended TOTP, or vice versa. The form should unregister the unused field when switching modes (`methods.unregister("totpCode")` / `methods.unregister("backupCode")`) or the submit handler should explicitly send only the relevant field.

findings.title: Zod schema makes password optional when totpEmail is present, but backup-code login still requires password on server
findings.body: The form schema sets `password: !!totpEmail ? z.literal("") : z.string().min(1)`. When arriving via the TOTP JWT flow (`totpEmail` set), the password field is hidden and empty. However, the server-side authorize() in `next-auth-options.ts` still verifies the password when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` — and when using a backup code, `credentials.totpCode` is empty, so the server WILL attempt password verification with an empty string and reject with `IncorrectEmailPassword`. This means the 'Lost access' backup-code flow is BROKEN for users arriving via the `totp` JWT redirect (external TOTP flow), because no password is collected but the server demands it. The backup-code branch on the server must either skip password verification when arriving via the TOTP JWT flow (trusting the JWT), or the login page must collect the password in backup-code mode. As written, a user who clicks 'Lost access' on the TOTP screen cannot log in with a backup code.

findings.title: E2E test uses prisma without importing it; test will fail at runtime
findings.body: The test references `prisma?.user.findFirst(...)` at lines 64 and 141, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (or similar) at the top of the file. The imports only include `@playwright/test`, `otplib`, `@calcom/lib/crypto`, `@calcom/lib/totp`, and `./lib/fixtures`. This will cause a ReferenceError at runtime when the 'Login with 2FA enabled' or 'Disable 2FA' steps execute. Add the missing prisma import.

findings.title: No test coverage for backup-code login or backup-code disable flows despite being the core feature
findings.body: The PR description says 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' and the test file even has a TODO: 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. The only backup-code-related test additions are UI checks for the download/copy/close buttons during setup. There is NO test that: (1) logs in using a backup code via the 'Lost access' flow, (2) verifies a used backup code cannot be reused, (3) disables 2FA using a backup code, or (4) verifies the backup-code branch in the disable endpoint. These are the primary new security-sensitive paths and they are completely untested. Add e2e tests that exercise backup-code login (including reuse rejection) and backup-code-based 2FA disable.

findings.title: Toggle button lacks type="button" and is inside a form, causing accidental form submission
findings.body: The 'Lost access' / 'Go back' toggle Button at line 113-121 is rendered inside a `<Form>` (which wraps a `<form>` element). The Button component likely defaults to `type="submit"` (common in this codebase's Button). Clicking 'Lost access' would submit the form, triggering `handleDisable` with empty/partial values instead of just toggling the state. Add `type="button"` to this Button to prevent implicit form submission.

findings.title: Download link wraps a Button in an anchor without preventing default or ensuring href is set before render
findings.body: The download `<a download="cal-backup-codes.txt" href={backupCodesUrl}>` wraps a `<Button>`. On the DisplayBackupCodes step, `backupCodesUrl` is set during `handleSetup` before `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayQrCode)`, so by the time the user reaches DisplayBackupCodes it should be populated. However, if the component re-renders before the state update completes, or if `backupCodesUrl` is empty string, the anchor has `href=""` and clicking it navigates to the current page. Additionally, nesting a `<button>` inside an `<a>` is invalid HTML (interactive content cannot be nested). Use a Button with `onClick` that programmatically triggers the download (e.g. creating a temporary anchor), or use an `<a>` styled as a button without a nested Button component.

findings.title: Setup endpoint returns plaintext backup codes in the API response and stores them encrypted as a single blob
findings.body: The setup endpoint returns `{ secret, keyUri, dataUri, backupCodes }` where `backupCodes` is the plaintext array. While this is necessary to display them once to the user, the codes are also persisted in the DB as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))` — a single encrypted blob containing all plaintext codes. This means: (1) the API response exposes all codes to anyone with a valid session (acceptable for setup, but should be rate-limited and ideally one-time), (2) the DB stores recoverable plaintext codes (encrypted at rest, but the encryption key is in env and the codes are not individually hashed), so a DB+env compromise reveals all backup codes. The endpoint also has no rate limiting — an authenticated user could call setup repeatedly (after disabling 2FA) to enumerate codes, though this is low risk. More importantly, the codes should be hashed before storage (store only hashes, return plaintext once), so that DB leaks do not expose usable backup codes.

findings.title: Third-party identity provider check is bypassed when backupCode is supplied
findings.body: The check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` only when `totpCode` is absent. If a user has a Google/SAML identity provider AND 2FA enabled (possible via the `loginWithTotp` flow for OAuth users), and an attacker supplies a `backupCode` (without `totpCode`), this check is skipped because `credentials.totpCode` is empty — wait, actually `!credentials.totpCode` is true when totpCode is empty, so the check WOULD throw. But then the next check `if (!user.password && user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` also throws `IncorrectEmailPassword`. However, if a backupCode is supplied, `credentials.totpCode` is empty, so both checks trigger and reject. The real issue: for OAuth users with 2FA, the backup-code flow requires `credentials.totpCode` to be empty (to pass the identity provider checks), but then the backup-code branch runs. This is actually consistent. The subtle bug: the condition `!credentials.totpCode` is used as a proxy for 'this is a first-factor-only attempt', but when a backupCode is supplied, totpCode is empty, so the identity-provider checks run — which is correct. However, the password check at line 121 `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` runs for backup-code attempts, meaning OAuth users (no password) with 2FA cannot use backup codes because `user.password` is null and the check is skipped, but then the backup-code branch runs without any first-factor verification. An OAuth user with 2FA enabled who arrives via `loginWithTotp` JWT has already proven identity via the JWT, so this is acceptable — but the logic is convoluted and fragile. The conditions should be restructured to explicitly handle the three cases: (1) first-factor only (email+password), (2) TOTP second factor, (3) backup code second factor, each with clear preconditions.

findings.title: Nested form element inside DialogContent Form creates invalid HTML and double submission handlers
findings.body: The `ConfirmPassword` step renders a `<form onSubmit={handleSetup}>` (line 172) INSIDE the outer `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} form={form}>` (line 209). This nests a `<form>` inside a `<form>`, which is invalid HTML — browsers will typically drop the inner form tag, causing `handleSetup` to never fire via form submission. The 'Continue' button at line 233 has `onClick={handleSetup}` AND `type="submit"`, so it works via the onClick, but pressing Enter in the password field may submit the outer form (triggering `handleEnable` with an empty totpCode) instead of `handleSetup`. This is a real UX bug: pressing Enter in the password field may trigger the wrong handler. The inner `<form>` should be removed and the password field should be part of the outer form, or the steps should be restructured to avoid nested forms.

findings.title: callbackUrl slash stripping regex is incorrect and can mangle valid URLs
findings.body: `if (/"\//.test(callbackUrl)) callbackUrl = callbackUrl.substring(1);` — the regex `/"\//` tests for a literal double-quote followed by a forward slash (`"/`), not just a leading slash. This was likely intended to be `/^\//` (leading slash). As written, it only strips the first character if the URL contains a `"/` sequence anywhere, which is wrong. A callbackUrl like `/booking` (leading slash, no quote) will NOT be stripped, then the next check `if (!/^https?:\/\//.test(callbackUrl))` prepends WEBAPP_URL, producing `https://app.cal.com//booking` (double slash). This is a pre-existing bug but is in the changed file and affects the login flow with backup codes. Fix the regex to `/^\//`.
